Sabatini DM.lab_name: Sabatini Group, IOCB Prague (Prague, Czech Republic)
Sabatini DM.role: Identified mTOR (as RAFT1) in 1994. His lab then mapped much of the machinery around it: raptor and rictor at the core of mTORC1 and mTORC2, the Rag–Ragulator system that docks mTORC1 on the lysosome, and the sensors that detect leucine, arginine and SAM
Sabatini DM.sub: IOCB Prague · Howard Hughes Medical Institute (2008–2021) · Whitehead Institute & MIT (1997–2021) · Born 1968, New York, USA
Sabatini DM.credit: Portrait: Ceal Capistrano/Whitehead Institute for Biomedical Research
story: David Sabatini grew up in a family of scientists — his father is a well-known cell biologist — and trained as an MD–PhD at Johns Hopkins in the laboratory of Solomon Snyder. As a graduate student he became fascinated by rapamycin, a drug found in the soil of Easter Island that could stop cells from growing. Nobody knew what it actually hit inside mammalian cells. In 1994 Sabatini answered that question: using rapamycin bound to its partner protein FKBP12 as 'bait', he fished a giant protein out of rat brain and named it RAFT1, the protein now called mTOR. That discovery opened the mammalian side of the field.

In 1997, still in his twenties, he started his own lab at the Whitehead Institute in Cambridge. Over the next two decades the Sabatini lab identified many core parts of the mTOR machine: the two complexes mTORC1 and mTORC2, the Rag GTPases and Ragulator that dock mTORC1 onto the lysosome, and — most strikingly — the actual protein sensors (Sestrin2, CASTOR1, SLC38A9, SAMTOR) that let a cell literally taste individual amino acids such as leucine and arginine. Together this work explained how our cells decide, moment to moment, whether there is enough food to grow.

His discoveries earned major honours including the Louisa Gross Horwitz Prize and the BBVA Frontiers of Knowledge Award. In 2021–2022 he left MIT and the Whitehead Institute. Since late 2023 he has led a laboratory at the Institute of Organic Chemistry and Biochemistry (IOCB) in Prague. The timeline below traces his scientific path through the studies collected in this Atlas.

highlights.SAB1994: Three years after yeast TOR, Sabatini purifies the Target Of Rapamycin (RAFT1/mTOR) from rat brain, proposing it as the direct target of FKBP12-rapamycin and a mammalian homolog of the yeast TOR proteins.
highlights.KIM2002: Defines mTOR Complex 1 by discovering raptor (reported in parallel by the Yonezawa and Avruch labs), the partner protein that makes mTOR sensitive to nutrients.
highlights.SAR2004: Discovers mTOR Complex 2 (via rictor, in parallel with Michael Hall's lab), a second, rapamycin-insensitive mTOR machine that controls the cytoskeleton.
highlights.SAN2008: Shows, in parallel with Kun-Liang Guan's lab, that the Rag GTPases are the switch that relays the amino-acid signal to mTORC1.
highlights.SAN2010: Ragulator docks mTORC1 onto the surface of the lysosome — pinpointing where nutrient sensing physically happens.
highlights.WOL2015: Identifies Sestrin2 as a direct leucine sensor for the mTORC1 pathway.
highlights.SAB2017: Sabatini's own 25-year retrospective on mTOR: uncovering the link from nutrients to growth.
highlights.KAN2013: Senior author of the finding that mTORC1 phosphorylation sites encode their own sensitivity to rapamycin and starvation, so one activity level can produce different output profiles.

Nobukuni T.lab_name: Tohoku Medical Megabank Organization, Tohoku University (Sendai, Japan)
Nobukuni T.role: Showed as first author that amino acids activate mTOR through the lipid kinase hVps34, by a route separate from insulin signalling through TSC, in parallel with a study from Jonathan Backer's laboratory
Nobukuni T.sub: Associate Professor, Tohoku Medical Megabank Organization, Tohoku University · Friedrich Miescher Institute for Biomedical Research, Basel (affiliation on NOB2005, 2005)
story: NOB2005 is written as an argument about evolution as much as about signalling. Its claim is that the amino-acid-driven TOR pathway came first, and that in animals the insulin/class I PI3K pathway was grafted onto it — so the two inputs should not be expected to run through the same machinery. Working in George Thomas's group at the FMI in Basel, Nobukuni showed that the amino acid signal to mTOR/raptor goes through class 3 PI3K (hVps34) rather than through the components of the insulin route.

The result matters for how the Atlas reads its own amino-acid branch. The Rag/Ragulator account that came later describes a different mechanism for the same input, and neither account has displaced the other; the corpus now carries both, with the disagreement stated rather than smoothed over.
His publication record after roughly 2019 is in population-scale health research at the Tohoku Medical Megabank rather than in mTOR signalling.

highlights.NOB2005: First author: amino acids signal to mTOR/raptor through class 3 PI3K, separately from the insulin/class 1 PI3K route.

Hurley JH.lab_name: Hurley Lab, UC Berkeley (Berkeley, California, USA)
Hurley JH.role: Structural biologist who uses cryo-EM to show how protein machines assembled on membranes control autophagy and nutrient signalling. His lab solved structures of the Rag–Ragulator complex and of the whole mTORC1–TFEB–Rag–Ragulator assembly on the lysosome
Hurley JH.sub: Professor of Molecular & Cell Biology and Kirsch Springer Chair in Biological Sciences, UC Berkeley (since 2013) · Faculty Scientist, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (since 2014) · Chief, Section on Structural Biology & Cell Signaling, NIDDK/NIH (1998–2013) · Senior Investigator, NIDDK/NIH (1997–2013) · Tenure-track Investigator, NIH (1992–1997) · Postdoctoral Fellow, University of Oregon (1990–1992) · PhD in Biophysics, UCSF (1990) · BA in Physics, San Francisco State University (1984) · Member, US National Academy of Sciences (2020) · Hans Neurath Award, Protein Society (2014)
story: mTORC1 only switches on when it is physically dragged to the surface of the lysosome, and the machine that does the dragging is a five-protein clamp called Ragulator together with the Rag GTPases. In the 2017 study, Hurley's laboratory solved the crystal structure of the whole human Ragulator at 1.4 angstrom resolution, which is sharp enough to see individual side chains. Lamtor1 turned out to wrap around the other four subunits like a belt, while the Lamtor2-Lamtor3 pair stacks on Lamtor4-Lamtor5 to build the platform the Rags sit on.

A crystal structure alone could not show where the Rags actually dock, so the team added two other methods. Hydrogen-deuterium exchange, which reports how exposed each stretch of protein is to water, mapped the Rag contact to the outer face of Lamtor2-Lamtor3 and to the floppy N-terminal tail of Lamtor1; electron microscopy then gave a lower-resolution picture of full-length RagA-RagC bound to Ragulator. Stitching these together produced a hybrid model in which the business ends of the Rags project away from the Ragulator core, held out like a handle for mTORC1 to grab.

Hurley spent two decades at the NIH before moving to Berkeley in 2013, and built his reputation on structures of the protein complexes that bend and cut membranes, especially the ESCRT machinery. His group now uses cryo-electron microscopy and cryo-electron tomography on the autophagy initiation machinery, on lysosome biology in cancer and Alzheimer's disease, and on how HIV hijacks membrane trafficking. The Ragulator work sits at the junction of those interests: it is a nutrient sensor, a membrane anchor and a drug-relevant target at the same time.

highlights.SUX2017: Senior author (with Roberto Zoncu); his laboratory determined the 1.4 angstrom Ragulator crystal structure and combined it with hydrogen-deuterium exchange and EM into the hybrid RagA/C-Ragulator model.
highlights.ESP2026: Co-author on the TBK1/ULK1-FNIP1-FLCN pathway that controls TFEB's release from the lysosome, independent of nutrient status.
